newsitem.title: USA: MSRB will hit obstacles as writes syndicate rules.
newsitem.headline: MSRB will hit obstacles as writes syndicate rules.

text.p: The Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board's upcoming efforts to tighten regulation of syndicate practices in the municipal bond market will be filled with obstacles, the panel's executive director said.

Christopher Taylor made the statement in a telephone press briefing on Friday, where he and MSRB Chairman Roger Hayes said the panel will focus soon on "concerns about practices in the formation of syndicates and selling groups and the pricing and allocation of bonds."
The board's plan follows an MSRB survey last summer of member firms on a range of topics lumped under the overall category "The Process for Underwriting Municipal Securities."
"There's stuff that came in on the survey that suggests there are concerns out there, and the board wants to be aggressive," Taylor said.
Taylor said that the board proposed detailed rules in 1976 and 1977 aimed at curbing price fixing and unfair bond allocations by municipal bond syndicates.

But the U.S. Justice Department, Federal Reserve Board and Securities and Exchange Commission made it clear that such direct controls on syndicate practices would run afoul of antitrust rules and the board's charter, Taylor said.
"That limits the possible options of what we might do, but the board still wants to look at the area," Taylor said.
Taylor said municipal industry changes make a new review timely.
"It's a much different industry than it was seven years ago in the late 1980s. There's much more involvement by the issuer in the allocation (and) the distribution of bonds," he said.
"Now that you have bigger bond funds, the whole distribution process since 1986 has really changed alot," Taylor said. "We want to go back and look at it again."
Taylor said the rules proposed by the board in 1976 and 1977 would have detailed how "the underwriting process could take place" and set "certain pricing restrictions."

"The rule said that there will be an order period, it shall not last longer than so and so, and during that period noone may sell bonds at anything other than the publicly reoffered price," Taylor said.

But SEC, Justice and the Federal Reserve said the rule would violate the MSRB's charter not to fix prices, Taylor said. "It stopped the board in its tracks from doing a rule that says here's how you should behave," Taylor said.
Instead, the board enacted rule G-11, which simply requires firms to make certain disclosures about their syndicate practices and within a specific timeframe, Taylor said.
Industry representatives said the board could write a rule that would increase the amount of disclosure by syndicates and tighten the timing of disclosure.
